content.text:
I've fixed the vulnerability. A URL starting with `//` (like `//google.com`) is no longer treated as absolute, so it gets added to `baseURL` instead of replacing it.

**Change:** In `lib/helpers/isAbsoluteURL.js`, the pattern now requires a scheme before the `//`. I made the scheme part `([a-z][a-z\d+\-.]*:)` required, where before it was optional (it had a `?`). I also updated the comment above it to explain why.

**Verification:** I used the setup from the issue, with a local server as `baseURL`, and requested `//example.invalid`. The request went to the base server at path `/example.invalid`, not to the outside host. The path ends up with one slash because axios already strips extra slashes when it joins the base URL and the path. The http adapter and regression unit tests pass (114 passing).

**One existing test will now fail:** `test/specs/helpers/isAbsoluteURL.spec.js:15` expects `isAbsoluteURL('//example.com/')` to be `true`. That assertion describes exactly the behaviour this fix removes, so it needs to expect `false`. I left it alone because you asked me not to change existing tests.

**Not covered:** I didn't change `lib/adapters/http.js`. With no `baseURL`, a request for `//host` is still resolved against `http://localhost`, which turns it into `http://host`. Making that throw an error would need the adapter to stop using `http://localhost` as a fallback, and that fallback is what currently lets plain relative paths like `/foo` work in Node. I kept the change small and didn't touch it.
